extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners interested in the theory and practice of comedy (dramaturgs, comic writers, literary critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and practical guidance for producing and recognizing comic effects and comic character-types on the stage or in literature, with focus on what makes something laughable and how to construct reproducible comic types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy aims at general types (not individuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy depicts characters as general types; it 'takes note of similarities' and 'aims at placing types before our eyes' rather than representing unique individualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and explanation: classical comedy titles (Le Misanthrope, L'Avare, Le Joueur) name whole classes of people; comic poets often surround a central character with satellites that are simplified copies of the same model to show the type in several instances. Contrast with tragedy, which concerns unique individualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic observation must be external and generalising
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic poet's method of observation is directed outwards, settling on the surface and producing results that are general rather than deeply individualised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This resembles inductive science: bring together analogous cases, extract their essence, and form an average/category. Comic observation should avoid deep probing into personality; it is 'skin-deep' and aims at features that can be noticed by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughable elements must be observable from without (unconscious in the subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is never ridiculous except through some mental attribute that is 'in some way absentminded' or lives on him 'without forming part of his organism' — i.e., something he does not perceive in himself but is visible to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: comic effects rely on the subject's lack of self-awareness; if the person recognizes the trait and it is fully integrated into self-consciousness, it ceases to be laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localise comic causes in an intermediate, immediately perceptible region
rubrics_metrics.description: To be laughable, the cause should be localised in some intermediate region of the soul — not so deep as to be inaccessible, nor so trivial as to be meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you penetrate too far into personality (deep causes), you endanger and may sacrifice all that was laughable. The cause should appear average and readily comparable across people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal attributes of a comic type (character specification)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideally comic type must be: deep-rooted yet superficial; invisible to its owner but visible to everyone else; extremely considerate to itself yet troublesome to others; immediately repressible but recurring; inseparable from social life; and capable of being attached to many vices or even virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This long checklist (Bergson's list) is a design template for creating sustainable comic characters: they must supply recurring material, be socially embedded, and be manifestly reproducible in others so laughter can correct them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity as the principal source of the laughable
rubrics_metrics.description: Vanity is identified as 'the mixture' most widely available for comic exploitation: superficial yet deep-rooted, yielding little real harm but persisting and drawing many vices into its orbit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vanity's features (gratitude for unreal services, resistance to conquest except by reflection) make it a reliable comic motive; laughter functions as a corrective to vanity and is the specific remedy for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's social function: laughter as corrective/reintegrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter serves to repress separatist tendencies, convert rigidity into plasticity, and readapt the individual to the whole — i.e., comedy's purpose is social correction and instruction as much as pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comedic situations with the aim of exposing and correcting social rigidity and absurd exclusiveness; the comic should help restore sociability by revealing and gently punishing deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ready-made social/professional categories for comic material
rubrics_metrics.description: Professions, trades, public services and other corporate groups form natural, ready-made comic categories because each impresses shared habits and peculiarities on its members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical device: exploit occupational stereotypes (professional vanity, jargon, special logic) to create group-based comic types; these categories are socially grounded and easily recognisable by audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional vanity and solemnity as comic traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who exalt their art or profession above all else exhibit professional vanity; when this merges with a priestly attitude about dubious arts, it becomes solemnity — a rich source of comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Moliere's doctors treating nature as an appendage to medicine; the stronger the quackery or dubiousness, the more inflated the solemnity and the greater the comic potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional callousness as a comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic character may display professional callousness by being so confined within the frame of his functions that he lacks ordinary human feeling (e.g., a judge indifferent to torture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to create coldly amusing detachment: the comic effect comes from treating human experiences as mere occupational routine ('Bah! cela fait toujours passer une heure ou deux').

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering profession-specific jargon and logic ludicrous in everyday contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Confine a profession within its own jargon or apply its specialised forms of reasoning to ordinary life to produce ludicrous effects; this often yields coarse comic effects but can be refined by adding character peculiarities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: translating scientific ideas into feminine sensibility (Les Femmes savantes) or a gambler using gambling metaphors for all relationships (Regnard's Joueur). The more the profession's language is misapplied, the more comic the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional logic (specialised reasoning) contrasted with common logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain ways of reasoning that are valid within a professional circle but implausible to outsiders produce comic effects when contrasted with universal/common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit mismatches between a group's internal logic and ordinary reasoning; the humour arises from the clash and the audience's recognition of the narrowness of that logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic requires reproducibility: choose peculiarities that form categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiarity observed should immediately appear as a category into which multiple individuals can step; comedy seeks traits that admit of self-repetition and hence general laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating characters, prefer traits that can naturally recur in several characters (satellites) to demonstrate the type and ensure the effect reaches many people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic effects can flow from high (subtle) elements to low (coarse) ones and vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple laughable image can infect more complex images; conversely, coarse comic effects sometimes result from a drop from a subtle comic element (e.g., attribution of vanity where it doesn't belong).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of reduction: subtle irony or vanity can be coarsened into crude visual contrast; the imaginative location of vanity in unexpected places often creates low comic effects (short man vs tall man as an attempt to 'raise himself').

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity in the comic must be of a definite kind (not 'absurdity in general')
rubrics_metrics.description: While some theories equate the comic with 'the logic of the absurd', Bergson argues that when absurdity occurs in comic it is a particular kind tied to the comic's cause; absurdity alone does not guarantee laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on raw contradiction or general absurdity; ensure the absurdity reflects the comic's specific origin (e.g., mechanical inelasticity of behaviour, privileged recollection imposing on changing reality) so it becomes laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic emerges from an arrest/rigidity of mental mobility (privileged recollection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense is the mind's mobility adapting ideas to objects; comic arises when a 'privileged recollection' is fixed in the mind and imposes itself on new circumstances (Don Quixote mistaking windmills for giants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct comic situations where an outdated/fixated idea is mechanically projected onto changing reality, producing a palpable disconnect between perception and object that the audience recognises as ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles and naming can signal typification
rubrics_metrics.description: Using generic titles or names that become common nouns ('a Tartuffe') signals to the audience that the character stands for a type rather than an irreducible individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider titling or naming strategies that prime the audience to read characters as representatives of a class; avoid names that remain exclusively proper when you wish to typify.
